deck.title: Double Entry Book-Keeping with Ledger Accounts

front_blocks.md: Define the **ledger**.

back_blocks.md: The **ledger** is the **collection of all the accounts** that a business keeps. It may be a physical book, a spreadsheet file or accounting software, with each account kept separately.

cards.front_md: Define the **ledger**.

front_blocks.md: Give two reasons why the ledger is divided into three.

back_blocks.md: Dividing the ledger:

- lets the **work be shared** among several people
- makes information **easier to find and check**, because the same types of account sit together
- helps **reduce fraud**, since gaps and errors show up more easily when different people keep different ledgers

front_blocks.md: Whose accounts are kept in the sales ledger?

back_blocks.md: The sales ledger holds the accounts of **all the credit customers**, which are the **trade receivables** accounts. Each customer has their own account showing what they owe the business.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

front_blocks.md: What is kept in the nominal ledger?

back_blocks.md: The **nominal ledger**, also called the general ledger, holds **every account except** those of the credit customers and credit suppliers. That includes sales and purchases, returns and discounts, every expense and income account, cash and bank, capital, drawings, inventory, and the non-current assets and liabilities.

front_blocks.md: Define the **double entry system**.

back_blocks.md: The **double entry system** records every transaction in **two accounts**, one as a **debit** entry and one as a **credit** entry. It keeps the accounting equation in balance and improves the accuracy of the financial statements.

cards.front_md: Define the **double entry system**.

front_blocks.md: How is a ledger account laid out, and what does each entry show?

back_blocks.md: Each account has two sides: **debit** entries on the **left**, sometimes labelled Dr, and **credit** entries on the **right**, labelled Cr. Every entry shows the **date**, the **details** and the **value** of the transaction.

The details column of a ledger account describes what the transaction was for.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The details column normally holds the **name of the other account** involved in the transaction. That is what lets a reader trace the matching entry on the other side of the double entry.

front_blocks.md: What does a debit entry do to an account?

back_blocks.md: A **debit** entry **increases an asset**, or **decreases a liability or the capital**. In terms of the accounting equation, it increases the left-hand side or decreases the right-hand side.

front_blocks.md: Why is an expense account debited when the business pays an expense?

back_blocks.md: An expense **reduces the profit**, and reducing the profit **reduces the capital**. A debit is what records a fall in capital, which is why every expense account is debited.

front_blocks.md: Why is an income account credited when the business receives income?

back_blocks.md: Income **increases the profit**, and increasing the profit **increases the capital**. A credit is what records a rise in capital, which is why sales, rent received and discount received are all credited.

front_blocks.md: A business sells goods on credit to a customer. Which account is debited and which is credited?

back_blocks.md: **Debit** the customer's **trade receivables** account, because they now owe more and that is an asset increasing. **Credit** the **sales** account, because sales increase profit and so increase capital.

front_blocks.md: The owner takes a business vehicle for personal use. Which account is debited and which is credited?

back_blocks.md: **Debit** the **drawings** account, because taking drawings reduces the capital. **Credit** the **vehicles** account, because the business now owns fewer vehicles and that is an asset decreasing.

front_blocks.md: Give two advantages of keeping double entry records.

back_blocks.md: Double entry records:

- make it **straightforward** to prepare the financial statements
- give an **accurate** figure for the profit or loss
- **reduce the possibility of fraud**
- give a bank or other lender **easy access** to the information they need

front_blocks.md: Define a **dishonoured cheque**.

back_blocks.md: A **dishonoured cheque** is a cheque the bank has **returned unpaid**. It usually means the payer did not have the funds to cover it, or that there was an error on the cheque such as a missing signature.

front_blocks.md: What is the principle behind recording a dishonoured cheque?

back_blocks.md: You make **exactly the same entries** as when the cheque was first recorded, but on the **opposite sides** of the accounts. That reverses the original transaction and puts the debt back where it was.

cards.front_md: What is the principle behind recording a dishonoured cheque?

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between issuing a credit note and giving a refund?
